# Guidance, Navigation, and Control {#navigation-overview}

Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) engineering is a multidisciplinary field. However, depending on the industry, application, and even the technology stack, the terminology can vary widely. This is largely an artifact of two different fields inventing and re-inventing very similar topics. Adding to this is the very fuzzy definition of what constitutes a robot, and where a simple machine ends and a robot begins. Here, we aim to make those definitions a little more clear.

## Terminology

The field of GNC engineering is concerned with the design, analysis, and implementation of systems that can guide, navigate, and control vehicles in a variety of environments semi- or fully-autonomously. This includes both manned and unmanned vehicles, as well as fully autonomous systems. Historically, the aerospace and marine industries have been the primary drivers of GNC engineering, with robotics being a more recent application that has gained significant attention in recent years but simultaneously seems to have slightly reinvented the field with new terminology. As such, while this is a robotics course, it is important to understand that the subject we're studying is in the field of autonomous GNC which sits at the intersection of traditional manned aerospace and maritime engineering (which uses semi-autonomous GNC systems) and in the unmanned robotics space. The primary difference between the two is in the terminology used to describe the problem, the specific applications and technologies used to solve it, and whether or not a human is in the decision making loop.

Generally, the aerospace and marine industries refer to the problem as guidance, navigation, and control. However, in the robotics industry, the problem is referred to as path planning, localization, and control. One of the goals of this course is to expand your horizons as to what constitutes a robotic or autonomous system and in the case of navigation, recognize that we’re drawing from a rich history of engineering and technology that has been developed in other industries. As such, I will frequently and often inadvertently interchange the terms guidance and navigation with path planning and localization. I will try to be consistent in my usage of the terms, but please be aware that the terms are often used interchangeably in the literature and in practice.

That said, control is pretty much always the same. If I start referring to control as something different, please inform my wife as I will have likely suffered a stroke.

So what do we mean by guidance, navigation, and control? At its most basic and general, *Guidance* or *Path Planning* involves the process of determining the path or trajectory that a vehicle or system should follow to achieve a specific goal from a set of initial conditions. This can involve determining the optimal path to minimize time, energy, or other resources, while avoiding obstacles and constraints. Guidance algorithms can be simple or complex, depending on the application and the level of autonomy required.

*Navigation* or *Localization* involves the process of determining the position, orientation, and velocity of a vehicle or system as it moves through space or operates in a given environment. This can involve using a variety of sensors and algorithms to estimate the state of the system, and can be done in real-time or offline. Navigation is critical for ensuring that the vehicle or system is able to follow the desired path or trajectory accurately and safely. Navigation is a specific realization of what is more broadly referred to as *state estimation* which is a form of probability that is used to estimate the values of a system using a combination of sensor measurements and mathematical models. State estimation is a fundamental concept in control theory and is used in a wide range of applications, including robotics, aerospace, and automotive systems.

*Control* involves the application of feedback and control algorithms to ensure that a system’s behavior conforms to a desired trajectory or set of performance criteria. Control theory is a branch of engineering and mathematics that deals with the behavior of dynamical systems and the design of systems to achieve desired performance or outputs. Control is critical for ensuring that the vehicle or system is able to follow the desired path or trajectory accurately and safely.

A very simple example based on the chart in @fig-gnc-path-states-control is as follows:

- Guidance is a complete path from A to B.
- Navigation is estimating the state along the path.
- Control is the set of arrows that specify the transition between navigation states.

## A Brief History of Navigation

### Navigation and the Earth and the Historical Problem of Navigation

All of navigation is with respect to an additional external reference frame, and can be very intuitive. The most common example of "navigation" is in giving directions to a person in an unfamiliar location. When giving such directions, we often rely on landmarks, cardinal directions, and distances to help the person reach their destination. The person being directed can then use these cues to estimate their position and orientation relative to the external reference frame (building, city, college campus, et cetera). Historically, this is how navigation (even large scale maritime navigation) was done for thousands of years. We would use landmarks, celestial bodies, and other cues to estimate our position and orientation relative to the Earth.

Such a model of navigation (barring celestial landmarks) generally presumes an external reference frame that is a three-axis orthonormal Cartesian frame where our inertial reference frame is aligned with the Earth’s gravity vector (z-axis) and our orientation is a direct single transformation from the reference frame to the body frame. Such an assumption is a valid and accurate approximation for small scale problems (indoors or well constrained). Large-scale navigation sees us navigating with respect to our position on the Earth, which is a bit more complicated.

Historically, navigation was done by dead reckoning where you periodically try to estimate your navigation states by observation of the external world (ex: observing a lighthouse). This is a very common method of navigation and is still used in many contexts today (e.g. hiking, driving, and at the most extreme: visual flight rules for aviation). However, the problem with dead reckoning is that it is very error prone and can lead to large errors over time. The primary culprit for this is the curvature of the Earth. The Earth is not flat, and as such, the distance you travel along the surface of the Earth (odometry) will not match the linear distance you would expect if the Earth were flat. This is because as you travel along the surface of the Earth, you are also traveling along a curved path, which means that your odometry will be greater than the linear distance you would expect if the Earth were flat.

This is a problem that has been known (and solved) for thousands of years. Ships going over the horizon are noted in writings from antiquity, and it was gradually discovered that the reason for this vertical deflection is the curvature of the Earth. The idea of a spherical Earth was postulated by Pythagoras in the 5th century BCE and later validated by Aristotle in the 3rd century BCE. The circumference of the Earth was first calculated by Eratosthenes in the 2nd century BCE using simple geometry and observations of the sun. Eratosthenes’ calculation was remarkably accurate: he estimated the circumference of the Earth to be approximately 40,000 kilometers, which is very close to the actual value of 40,075 kilometers at the equator, and 40,008 kilometers across the poles. The fact that the Earth is not a perfect sphere, but rather an ellipsoid, was noted later as measurements became more precise.

The Earth's curvature is perceptible at a linear distance of approximately 6.2 km (3m). This means that if you were to travel 6.2 km along the surface of the Earth, you would be 3 meters above the linear distance you would expect if the Earth were flat. Alternatively, a three meter tall object will be completely obscured behind the curvature at a linear distance of a round seven kilometers. Dan Olsen of *Folding Ideas* did a [really great demonstration of this](https://youtu.be/JTfhYyTuT44?si=yto8fDeufJ65PBF0&t=585). For most practical navigation purposes, the flat-Earth approximation is valid up to about 10 km (7.84m deflection), which means that for distances less than 10 km, we can safely assume that the Earth is flat and that our odometry will match our linear distance. However, for distances greater than 10 km, we need to take into account the curvature of the Earth in order to accurately estimate our position and orientation. We will get into the mathematics of how to do this later in the course, but for now, it’s important to understand that the curvature of the Earth and the orientation of the gravity vector is a fundamental problem that has been known for thousands of years and has had a significant impact on navigation throughout history.

![Geometry of Earth's curvature and vertical deflection (vertical scale exaggerated for clarity). Traveling an arc length $s$ along the curved surface from $A$ to $B$ leaves you a distance $d$ below the tangent ("flat-Earth") line through $A$, where $(R+d)^2 = R^2 + s^2$ and, since $s \ll R$, $d \approx s^2/(2R)$.](../../images/earth-curvature-deflection.png){#fig-earth-curvature}

Celestial observations made more sense when viewed from an understanding of a spherical Earth, and partially contributed to a greater inclination towards heliocentrism. While certainly an important scientific and mathematical development that obviously has a substantial impact on navigation, the discovery of the Earth’s curvature and the development of a spherical model of the Earth had impacts far beyond navigation. It was a fundamental shift in our understanding of the world and our place in it. It challenged long-held beliefs and paved the way for new scientific discoveries and technological advancements. It also had profound philosophical and cultural implications, as it forced us to reconsider our relationship with the natural world and our place in the cosmos. This accurate spherical model of the Earth also enabled the development of more accurate maps and navigation tools, which in turn facilitated exploration, trade, and cultural exchange.

Celestial navigation was also developed as a method of navigation that relies on observations of celestial bodies (e.g. the sun, moon, stars, and planets) to determine position and orientation. This method of navigation was particularly useful for maritime navigation, as it allowed sailors to navigate across open oceans where there were no landmarks to rely on. Celestial navigation relies on the fact that the positions of celestial bodies are predictable and can be used as reference points to determine position and orientation. By measuring the angles between celestial bodies and the horizon, sailors could determine their latitude and longitude. This method of navigation was widely used until the development of more advanced navigation technologies in the 20th century.

### Where does this leave us? {#modern-navigation}

The accurate spherical model and navigation by celestial observations and physical landmarks was a sufficient form of navigation for thousands of years, and is still used in many contexts today. The development of more advanced navigation technologies in the 20th century has certainly made navigation easier and more accurate, but it’s important to recognize that the fundamental principles of navigation have been known for thousands of years and have been used by countless generations of navigators to explore and navigate the world around us. Keep in mind, with basic knowledge of celestial navigation, a spherical Earth, and sailing, peoples from east Asia were able to navigate and migrate into the Pacific Islands thousands of years ago (circa 3,500 to 1,500 BCE).

However, as we begin to enter into the advent of the industrial revolution and the development of faster means of transportation (even if maritime travel is still sail and wind based) there is an increasing need for more accurate and reliable navigation methods. At this point, we have a good understanding of the Earth's curvature and reliable method to calculate latitude. However, longitude is still a problem. Longitude proved notoriously difficult to measure: you’re measuring the angular displacement between your position and a fixed reference point that you can’t see and is entirely arbitrary, even more so when at sea. The primary method for calculating longitude was through celestial navigation, which relies on the observation of celestial bodies to determine position and orientation. However, this method is not always reliable, especially in poor weather conditions or when the celestial bodies are not visible. Additionally, the development of faster means of transportation (e.g. steam-powered ships) made it more difficult to rely on celestial navigation, as it requires frequent observations and calculations to maintain an accurate estimate of position and orientation.

Things pick back up during the European Renaissance after the re-discovery of classical texts preserved in the Middle East by Persian and Arab scholars (as well as refinement and contributions of their own). This invigorates and inspires European scientists. Galileo Galilei, during the 15th and 16th century, lays some of these foundations for early mechanics (pendulum, gravitational constant), and proposes a way to calculate longitude using the orbital periods of Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto (moons of Jupiter). Building off of Galileo’s work, Giovanni Domenico Cassini (1668) publishes detailed tables of Jupiter’s moons enabling useful and accurate calculation of longitude on land. René Descartes creates an early postulation for the conservation of momentum (1644), followed by Wallis (1668) and ultimately capped off by Sir Isaac Newton (1687) with the discovery of the laws of motion and gravitation that explains an elliptical model of the Earth.

So, by around 1,700 C.E. we have all the required mathematics to describe our elliptical Earth and measure and describe our relative position and motion on it provided we are on land. The primary limiting factor for celestial longitude measurements was due to the fact that they would need to be compared across different locations. Thus longitude information was not readily available in real time. For a time of increasingly fast maritime travel, this was a problem. To begin to understand the problem, we need to understand that longitude is essentially a measure of time. Classical landmark-based navigation relies on landmarks being at the same place and not moving. It is still technically possible to use moving landmarks to navigate (e.g. ocean tides) however the timing of these events needs to be precisely measured and the physical space needs to be well understood. Longitude does not have either of these properties readily available.

To help in your understanding of this problem, consider the modern notion of "time zones" and work backwards. The Earth is divided into 24 time zones, each of which is approximately 15 degrees of longitude wide. This means that if you are in a time zone that is one hour ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), you are approximately 15 degrees east of the prime meridian. However, if you are an average person in the 17th century, and a journey from Madrid to Paris takes you several days, you have no real notion or perception of the fact that you are crossing time zones: the sun rises and sets each day. However in this modern age where travel and communication across such vast distances is commonplace, we have a much greater need to understand the relative differences in time across different locations.

However if you invert this problem and use the one consisten landmark that is the same everywhere (the sun) and measure the time of a specific event (e.g. solar noon) you can calculate your longitude by comparing the local time of that event to the time at a fixed reference point (e.g. Greenwich Mean Time). This inextricably links the problem of navigation to the problem of timekeeping. The Dutch polymath Gemma Frisius, first postulated such a solution in 1530 and introduced the idea of a marine chronometer to solve the problem of longitude. The idea is that if you have a precise measurement of the time at a fixed location (e.g. London, Paris, Amsterdam), you can calculate your relative rotation using the known rotation rate of the Earth (360 degrees per 24 hours) and a measurement of a known celestial body at its apogee (typically solar noon). For example, if it is solar noon locally (12:00) and your chronometer reads 1pm (13:00), you are 1/24 of a rotation behind your reference and thus at 15 degrees longitude west.

As an aside: pay no mind to the historic convention of degrees of latitude and longitude being further subdivided into minutes and seconds. Whereas one hour of time approximately corresponds to fifteen degrees of longitude, the further subdivisions do not correspond or correlate to units of time. Prefer the modern decimal degree notation for latitude and longitude, which is more intuitive and easier to work with.

The marine chronometer fundamentally changes the longitude problem to one of developing a precise timekeeping device that can be mobile and long lasting and preferably be used at sea. This means you can't use other common timekeeping devices at the time: can’t use a pendulum or flowing water or sand on a swaying ship. You can't rely on a sundial, because you need to be able to calculate longitude at night and in poor weather conditions.

Because of its association with maritime trade and commerce, not to mention the military applications, this was both a highly valuable and highly difficult problem to solve. Multiple prizes were offered by various European governments to provide a means of accurate calculation. Spain issued a prize in 1598 worth 6,000 ducts (approximately \$1.3 million USD in 2023), and the Netherlands offered a prize of 10,000 florins (approximately \$60 million USD in 2023). Most notably, Great Britain established the Longitude Rewards in 1714 with prizes of £10,000 (approximately £1.6 million, or \$2 million USD in 2023) for a measurement of longitude with accuracy up within 1 degree (60 nautical miles, approximately 110 km at the equator), £15,000 (approximately £2.4 million, or \$3 million USD in 2023) for accuracy within 40 minutes (40 nautical miles, approximately 74 km at the equator), and £20,000 (approximately £3.2 million, or \$4 million USD in 2023) for accuracy within 30 minutes (30 nautical miles, approximately 55 km at the equator).

This lead to the creation of the “sea watch” by John Harrison (1720s-1770s). The final version submitted was accurate to approximately 1.25 minutes (approximately 1 nautical mile) on a transatlantic journey. Mr. Harrison was awarded a total of £23,065 (\~\$3.6 million over 50 years) for both development and in successfully won prizes. Unfortunately, due to political reasons, he was never awarded the full amount of the prize money. Despite his significant contributions to the field of navigation and timekeeping, Harrison faced significant challenges in receiving the recognition and compensation he deserved for his work.

While a significant advancement in navigation and timing, the marine chronometer was still not a perfect solution. It was expensive, bulky, and required regular maintenance. Additionally, it was still reliant on celestial observations to determine longitude, which could be difficult in poor weather conditions or when the celestial bodies were not visible. Furthermore, measurements were still slow and infrequent, as they required manual observations of fixed events and hand calculations. This meant that navigation was still a slow and error-prone process, especially for long-distance voyages, but nonetheless useful for slow-moving vessels that would take weeks to months to cross long distances. With steam powered ships and flight proving to be viable methods of transportation going into the 20th century, we are pushing the edge of what is viable by navigating with these methods.

When it comes down to it, by the early 20th century, we’re still only really updating based on position measurements (no direct measures of velocity, odometry is even less reliable for sea and air travel), with measurements that can only be taken under fair conditions with clear skies once or twice a day. Calculations of velocity is slow and must be derived from several observations. This is not sufficient for the needs of modern navigation, especially for fast-moving vehicles like airplanes and ships. The need for more accurate and reliable navigation methods becomes increasingly apparent as we enter the 20th century and beyond. That said, we can still leverage our understanding of physics and mathematics: we know through calculus that we can also take the inverse approach to finding position by integrating higher order derivatives to arrive at the base state. Dynamics tells us that we can control the motion of an object by imparting force on it to accelerate it. We can sometimes measure the force output of a system, but that still leaves other variables (namely mass). For vehicles, these control systems are largely open loop, we can command a throttle percentage, but can’t accurately tell how fast we’re going until we can measure our position again.

Enter the inertial measurement unit (IMU) in 1950. The IMU is a sensors that attempts to measure and compute internal states directly from the perspective of the vehicle, and then use physics and calculus to derive the navigation states. The IMU is a combination of accelerometers and gyroscopes that measure specific forces (accelerations) and angular rates (angular velocities) respectively. By integrating these measurements over time, we can estimate the position, velocity, and orientation of the vehicle. This allows for continuous navigation even in the absence of external reference points, making it particularly useful for applications such as aerospace and marine navigation where external cues may be limited or unreliable.

This course will start from the basis of an IMU for navigation. While useful, IMUs are notoriously noisy and error prone sensors, and there is a large body of work for how to integrate these sensors into navigation systems. We will cover some of the basics of how to use an IMU for navigation, as well as some of the more advanced techniques for integrating IMU measurements with other sensors (e.g. GPS, cameras, et cetera) to improve navigation accuracy and reliability.
